transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you into the clinic today?

Well, I... I came in because my manager told me I needed to. I got written up last week. It’s just, at the register, I keep getting stuck doing these things that don’t really fit the moment? Like, I’ll start tapping the barcode scanner in a certain pattern, or I’ll just freeze completely with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer while the customer is waiting. 

And people hate waiting. They get so huffy over their groceries. I see what people buy all day, you know, it’s mostly frozen dinners and those little energy shots. I used to drink so much black coffee when I was getting my bachelor's degree—I studied history, actually. Fascinating stuff, especially the Industrial Revolution. Factories really changed how humans perceive time. Time just moves differently now, everything is measured by the clock instead of the sun. It makes you wonder how we ever adapted to it. 

But anyway, yeah, the manager got mad about the freezing thing and wrote me up.
When you freeze or find yourself tapping like that, what is going through your mind?

I... I’m not really sure. It’s not like I’m planning to do it, so I don't really know what's in my head. Sometimes it’s just completely blank, or I’m just focusing on the red light of the scanner. 

It’s a laser, you know. We use them to ring up frozen peas now, but it’s actually incredible technology. Einstein theorized the foundation for lasers way back in 1917. I read a biography on him a few years ago. Did you know he stopped wearing socks? He said his big toe would always just poke a hole in them anyway, so he just gave up on them entirely. Which makes sense, really. The quality of textiles has completely plummeted. You buy a pack of socks today and they’re threadbare in a month. It all goes back to the shift in the garment industry during the mid-twentieth century when synthetic fibers were introduced... 

But, um, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh. Yeah, I don't really notice any specific thoughts when I freeze up. It just kind of happens.
Have you noticed any change in how much sleep you need lately?

Sleep? No, not really. I mean, I sleep about the same as I always do. Usually I just lie down and eventually it happens. I actually got a new mattress a couple of years ago because the springs in the old one were poking me right in the ribs. It's memory foam. They originally invented memory foam for NASA, you know, for the airplane seats to absorb the shock. It's wild how much stuff we use every day that came from the space program. Like scratch-resistant lenses and those foil blankets they give marathon runners. I've never run a marathon, my knees could never take it. The human knee is a terrible design, really. We started walking upright and the joint just wasn't built to bear all that weight long-term. It's an evolutionary compromise. 

But, uh, no, my sleep is fine. I haven't noticed needing more or less of it.
When you freeze like that, are you still aware of people talking or moving around you?

Aware? Um... yeah, I think so. I mean, I hear the customer sighing, or the cart rattling. It's just that I can't seem to make my hand move. It's like the signal from my brain gets stuck somewhere along the way. The nervous system is basically just electrical impulses, right? It's kind of like the old telegraph lines they used to have strung up everywhere. Samuel Morse sent the first message in 1844. "What hath God wrought." Pretty dramatic for a first text message, if you think about it. Now people just send an emoji of a thumbs up. Language is devolving, really. We're going right back to hieroglyphics. The ancient Egyptians used symbols for everything, and they built the pyramids, so maybe it's not a bad thing. They say the workers who built the pyramids were actually paid in beer. Three rations of beer a day. Which sounds like a terrible idea for workplace safety, especially when you're moving two-ton blocks of limestone... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, right. Yeah, I hear them, I just... I just stay stuck.
Have you been diagnosed with any medical conditions or physical health problems?

Medical conditions? Um, no, I don't think so. I haven't been to a regular doctor in a while, honestly. Last time I went was... gosh, years ago for a physical. They always make you wear those paper gowns. I don't understand why they haven't invented something better than tissue paper to cover you up. It's so humiliating, and it tears if you just shift your weight on the exam table. Paper manufacturing is actually a fascinating process, though. The Chinese invented it back in the Han dynasty, using mulberry bark and hemp. Before that, people were writing on bamboo slips, which seems incredibly heavy to carry around. Imagine trying to carry a novel made of bamboo. You'd need a wheelbarrow just to read a book. Books are getting shorter anyway, nobody has the attention span anymore. People just scroll through their phones for hours. The blue light from those screens really messes with your circadian rhythm, which is probably why everyone is so tired all the time... 

Anyway, um, no, no physical health problems that I know of. I'm pretty healthy, I guess.
When you freeze like that, if someone tries to move your arm, what happens?

If someone tries to move my arm? Well, if they pull on it, it kind of just... stays where they put it, you know? But usually people don't touch me. They just stare. It's why I came in, actually, because at the register I keep getting stuck doing things that don't fit the moment. Like, I'll be tapping the scanner in a pattern, or freezing with my hand over the cash drawer while the customer is waiting. Cash drawers are so outdated anyway. Everything is tap-to-pay now. The chips in those cards are basically microcomputers. They have more processing power than the computers that sent Apollo 11 to the moon. Neil Armstrong stepping out on that dust... I wonder if moon dust smells like anything? They say space smells like seared steak and hot metal. I don't eat much steak anymore, red meat is bad for your cholesterol. My uncle had terrible cholesterol, he had to take statins for twenty years. Statins are synthesized from fungi, originally. Fungi are more closely related to animals than plants, which is why mushrooms have that meaty texture...

But, uh, yeah, last week getting stuck like that got me written up by my manager. So, that's why I'm here.
